vignettes.body:
Ryan Tan is the chief investment officer of an endowment portfolio. The portfolio has 20% of its assets invested in two hedged funds, with an equal proportion invested in each fund. The investment strategies used by the two hedge funds are as follows.
Fund 1 uses equity market-neutral strategies
Fund 2 applies an event-driven strategy focusing on distressed securities
The endowment is considering investing in just one hedge fund. Tan performs a scenario analysis to better understand relative performance if the entire 20% allocation is invested in one fund. For this analysis, Tan considers a third hedge fund for possible investment. Tan's objective is to select the fund that would maximize the endowment portfolio's risk-adjusted return, where risk is defined as downside deviation. Exhibit 1 shows the risk-return characteristics of the overall portfolio with a 20% allocation to either Fund 1, Fund 2, or Fund 3.
Exhibit 1
#  | Standard Deviation | Sharpe Ratio | Sortino Ratio
Allocation to Fund 1 | 8.2% | 0.81 | 1.5
Allocation to Fund 2 | 8.3% | 0.82 | 1.3
Allocation to Fund 3 | 7.9% | 0.80 | 1.4
Finally, Tan evaluates whether it would be better to reallocate the endowment's 20% hedge funds investment to Fund 4, a fund-of-funds. This allocation would give the endowment portfolio exposure to multiple distinct hedge fund strategies.

questions.q: The investment strategy used by Fund 1 most likely:
options: applies a higher level of leverage.
delivers returns that are more volatile than other hedge fund strategies.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Fund 1 follows an equity market neutral (EMN) strategy, and the main source of skill for an EMN manager is in security selection, with market timing being of secondary importance.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Fund 1 follows an equity market neutral (EMN) strategy, and EMN managers generally are more useful for portfolio allocation during periods of non-trending or declining markets because they typically deliver returns that are steadier and less volatile than those of many other hedge strategy areas.

questions.q: The investment strategy used by Fund 2 most likely:
options: has a short initial lock-up period.
produces either very good or very bad results.
applies primarily to short selling and is short biased.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Fund 2 follows an event-driven strategy focusing on distressed securities. By nature, distressed debt and other illiquid assets may take several years to resolve, and they are generally difficult to value. Therefore, hedge fund managers running portfolios of distressed securities typically require relatively long initial lock-up periods (e.g., no redemptions allowed for the first two years) from their investors.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Fund 2 follows an event-driven strategy focusing on distressed securities. Distressed funds normally take long positions in investments and are often forced to sell at distressed prices that reflect increased credit and liquidity risks. Specifically, as noted in the curriculum: Outright shorts or hedged positions are possible, but distressed securities investing is usually long-biased. It is subject to security-specific outcomes.

questions.q: Based on his definition of risk and his objective to maximize the endowment's risk-adjusted return, Tan should allocate to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the hypothetical combined portfolio where the endowment invests only in Fund 2 has the highest Sharpe ratio but not the highest Sortino ratio. For hedge fund strategies with large negative events, the Sortino ratio is considered a better performance measure.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the hypothetical combined portfolio where the endowment invests only in Fund 3 has the lowest standard deviation of returns but not the highest Sortino ratio. For hedge fund strategies with large negative events, the Sortino ratio is considered a better performance measure.

questions.q: The reallocation of hedge fund investments to Fund 4 would most likely:
options: result in an additional layer of principal-agent relationships.

Judy West is a trader who is training a new hire, Alex Carter, on the application of option pricing models.
West and Carter first discuss how to estimate the value of a European-style call option using a two-period binomial model on a non-dividend paying stock. The inputs are:
current stock price (S) is $100
exercise price (X) is $100
up factor (u) is 1.4, down factor (d) is 0.7
risk-free rate is 3%
West then reviews the Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) model and presents information in Exhibit 1. She explains this information can be used to structure a delta hedge for option positions. West presents an example of delta hedging a short call position on 5,000 shares of an underlying stock. She asks Carter to determine the optimal number of shares of stock to buy to hedge the short call position.

West next sets up a gamma hedging exercise. She shows Carter how to predict the change in call price for a given change in the underlying stock price for the three calls in Exhibit 2. All three calls have the same time to expiration. West explains how including gamma improves the accuracy of the prediction.

vignettes.body:
Mary Navarro, a portfolio manager, is analyzing the effect of current macroeconomic factors on various asset classes and is researching actively managed funds.
Navarro first evaluates the effect of macroeconomic factors on the P/E ratio and the performance of equities. She considers the following three scenarios over the next 10 years:
Scenario 1: Real GDP growth volatility and inflation expectations both increase.
Scenario 2: There is declining uncertainty about future inflation.
Scenario 3: Expected real earnings growth and the equity risk premium both increase.
Navarro next reviews the performance of an active portfolio that does not have any short-selling restrictions. Exhibit 1 summarizes the returns, allocations, and performance statistics for the active portfolio and the benchmark. Using this information, Navarro evaluates the sources of value added.
Exhibit 1
# | Portfolio Return | Portfolio Allocation | Benchmark Return | Benchmark Allocation
Equities | 10% | 70% | 8% | 60%
Fixed income | 4% | 30% | 5% | 40%
Performance statistics
# | Portfolio | Benchmark
Active return | 1.40% | ---
Active risk | 10.00% | ---
Standard deviation | 21% | 17%
Sharpe ratio | 0.29 | 0.28
Navarro believes that the realized performance statistics in Exhibit 1 are reasonable estimates for the future. She determines that the optimal level of active risk is 8.50% and investigates whether the Sharpe ratio of the active portfolio can be improved by combining investments in this portfolio and the benchmark.
Several months later, Navarro reviews three recent developments regarding the active portfolio in Exhibit 1. Using the expanded fundamental law of active management, Navarro evaluates the effect of the following events on the information ratio of the active portfolio.
Event 1: The portfolio rebalancing frequency has been changed from semiannual to quarterly.
Event 2: The portfolio manager has added two analysts with strong forecasting ability.
Event 3: Short-selling restrictions have been added to the portfolio's IPS.

questions.q: Which of the following scenarios would most likely result in a decrease in the P/E ratio for equities?
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because declining uncertainty about future inflation would result in a higher P/E ratio.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the two factors in this scenario (i.e., an expectation of higher real earnings growth and a higher equity risk premium) would have opposite effects on the P/E ratio, resulting in an indeterminate conclusion.

questions.q: For the active portfolio, the value added attributable to security selection is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the value added attributable to asset allocation, which can be calculated as shown below:

[2]	Benchmark allocation
[3]	Difference in allocation
[4] = [2] – [3]	[1] × [4]

Fixed income	5%	30%	40%	–10%	–0.5%
Asset allocation = Total	0.3%
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this answer uses benchmark allocation weights instead of portfolio allocation weights, as shown below:

[1]	Benchmark return
[2]	Value added

[4]	[3] × [4]
Equities	10%	8%	2%	60%	1.2%
Fixed income	4%	5%	–1%	40%	–0.4%
Total	0.8%
C. Correct.

questions.q: Can Navarro improve the Sharpe ratio of the active portfolio by combining investments in this portfolio and the benchmark?
options: Yes, by taking a short position in the active portfolio and a long position in the benchmark
Yes, by taking a long position in the active portfolio and a short position in the benchmark
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the active portfolio's expected active risk is not at its optimal level, therefore the expected Sharpe ratio is not at its maximum value.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the optimal amount of active risk (8.5%) is less than the expected active risk of the active portfolio (10.00%). This answer would only be correct if that relation were reversed.

questions.q: Which of the following events will most likely reduce the information ratio of the active portfolio?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this event increases the information ratio (IR). Increasing the rebalancing frequency (from semiannual to quarterly) increases the number of independent decisions made, which increases breadth (BR) and thus the information ratio.
IR = (TC) (IC) BR0.5
BR measures the number of independent decisions made per year by the investor in constructing the portfolio. A higher (lower) rebalancing frequency implies a higher (lower) BR. It is important to note that doubling the rebalancing frequency probably does not double BR due to the lack of independence among decisions.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this event increases the information ratio (IR). Adding two analysts with strong forecasting ability increases the information coefficient (IC).
IR = (TC) (IC) BR0.5
IC measures the forecasting ability of the fund manager. The stronger the link between forecasted active returns and realized returns, the higher the IC.
This event will also increase breadth (BR) because the additional research provided by the two analysts will most likely increase the number of independent decisions made during the year. As a result, the information ratio increases.
C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Malte Kaufmann is an equity analyst initiating coverage on several listed stocks.
First, Kaufmann determines the sustainable growth rates for Company A and Company B using the PRAT model. Company A and Company B have identical total asset turnover ratios, but Company A has a higher payout ratio, higher profit margin, and higher equity multiplier. Based on the PRAT model, Kaufmann concludes that Company A has a lower sustainable growth rate than Company B.
Kaufmann uses the two-stage DDM to value Company B's shares, which are currently trading at EUR 42.37. He forecasts that the current dividend (D0) of EUR 1.40 will grow by 12% per year for the next two years. Thereafter, Kaufmann assumes that the growth rate will decline to 6% and remain at that level indefinitely. He estimates the required return on equity to be 10%. Kaufmann considers a share to be fairly valued if its price is within +/–5% of the estimated model value.
Next, Kaufmann considers three companies to add to his list of covered firms. Based on the historical data in Exhibit 1, which covers the 5-year period up to the most recent year (Year 0), Kaufmann assesses which of the three companies is most suitable for valuation using the Gordon growth model.
Exhibit 1

Finally, Kaufmann calculates residual income for Company C in the current year. He uses the following information for Company C:

questions.q: Kaufmann's conclusion about the sustainable growth rate of Company A relative to Company B is best supported by Company A's:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because a higher profit margin will lead to a higher sustainable growth rate based on the PRAT model, which calculates the growth rate as the product of retention rate, profit margin, asset turnover, and equity multiplier (leverage). Company A has a higher profit margin.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because a higher equity multiplier will lead to a higher sustainable growth rate based on the PRAT model, which calculates the growth rate as the product of retention rate, profit margin, asset turnover, and equity multiplier (leverage). Company A has a higher equity multiplier.

questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the current share price of EUR 42.37 is within the tolerance band of +/–5% relative to the model value of EUR 41.34.
An undervaluation results if the cash flows are not discounted:
The next three dividends are calculated as follows.
D(1) = 1.40 × 1.12 = 1.568
D(2) = 1.568 × 1.12 = 1.75616
D(3) = 1.75616 × 1.06 = 1.86153
Based on D(3), the value at t = 2 of the dividends from t = 3 until infinity (terminal value) can be calculated using the Gordon growth model: V(2) = 1.86153/(0.10 – 0.06) = 46.53824.
Next, the two dividends and the terminal value are added up: 1.568 + 1.75616 + 46.53824 = 49.8624 ≈ 49.86.
Calculating the deviation of the current share price from the intrinsic value:
42.37/49.86 – 1 = –0.150262 ≈ –15.0%. The shares are undervalued by 15.0%. 
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the current share price of EUR 42.37 is within the tolerance band of +/–5% relative to the model value of EUR 41.34.
An overvaluation results if only the terminal value is discounted: 
The next three dividends are calculated as follows.
D(1) = 1.40 × 1.12 = 1.568
D(2) = 1.568 × 1.12 = 1.75616
D(3) = 1.75616 × 1.06 = 1.86153
Based on D(3), the value at t = 2 of the dividends from t = 3 until infinity (terminal value) can be calculated using the Gordon growth model: V(2) = 1.86153/(0.10 – 0.06) = 46.53824.
This terminal value is discounted at the required return on equity: 
46.53824/1.12 = 38.46136 ≈ 38.46. 
Calculating the deviation of the current share price from the intrinsic value:
42.37/38.46 – 1 = 0.101625 ≈ 10.2%. The shares are overvalued by 10.2%.

vignettes.body:
Darren Carter is a credit analyst reviewing Gowran Bank. The bank is subject to the Basel III regulatory framework and prepares its financial statements under IFRS.
Carter first considers Gowran's capital adequacy. For the most recent year end, Gowran reported Common Equity Tier 1 Capital of $15 billion and risk-weighted assets of $100 billion. Carter determines Gowran's pro forma year-end Common Equity Tier 1 Capital ratio to account for the following two events, which occurred after the most recent year end.
Gowran issued $1 billion of Additional Tier 1 Capital.
The regulator required Gowran to recognize an additional $3.5 billion of operational risk-weighted assets.
Carter next assesses Gowran's asset quality by analyzing the adequacy of its allowance for loan losses. Specifically, he examines how the ratio of the bank's allowance for loan losses to non-performing loans changed during the most recent year based on the data (in millions) in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
Non-performing loans at start of year | $2,000
Non-performing loans at end of year | $2,400
Allowance for loan losses at start of year | $1,500
Provision for loan losses during the year | $500
Charge-offs, net of recoveries, during the year | $200
Gowran has a defined benefit pension plan (Plan A) that is closed to new members. Carter determines the effect of this pension plan on Gowran's income statement.
As part of its executive management compensation, Gowran also has a stock option plan (Plan B). Three years ago, Gowran granted executives 5 million at-the-money stock options with a three-year vesting period. On the grant date, Gowran's share price was $12 and the fair value of each option was $3. All of the options are now vested in the current year. Carter determines the effect on Gowran's paid-in capital on its balance sheet in the current year, assuming that 2 million of the stock options are exercised at the strike price of $12 and Gowran's share price is currently $18.

questions.q: Gowran's pro forma Common Equity Tier 1 Capital ratio is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this indicates that neither of the actions that occurred after year end affected the Common Equity Tier 1 Capital Ratio (i.e., $15 billion / $100 billion = 15.0%)
While the issuance of Additional Tier 1 Capital is correctly excluded from the Common Equity Tier 1 Capital Ratio, the additional operational risk-weighted assets should be included. The latter might be assumed to be true if the only type of risk-weighted assets related to credit risk and while it is typically the largest component of risk-weighted assets for a bank, it is not the only type.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this would be the pro forma Common Equity Tier 1 Capital ratio at year end for Gowran if both actions occurring after year end were assumed to have an effect on the ratio as follows: ($15 billion + $1 billion) / ($100 billion + $3.5 billion) = 15.46% ~ 15.5%.

questions.q: Over the most recent year, the ratio of Gowran's allowances for loan losses to non-performing loans:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because over the past year, the ratio of Gowran's allowances for loan losses to non-performing loans did not change. 
The conclusion that the ratio decreased could be derived if provision for loan losses during the year was subtracted rather than added when calculating the allowance for loan losses at the end of the year.
Allowance for loan losses at start of year	1,500
Subtract: Provision for loan losses during the year	500
Subtract: Net charge-offs during the year	200
Allowance for loan losses at end of year	800
Then the calculation of the ratio of allowances for loan losses to non-performing loans becomes;
 	Start of Year	End of Year
Allowances for loan losses	1,500	800
Non-performing loans	2,000	2,400
Ratio	0.75	0.33
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because over the past year, the ratio of Gowran's allowances for loan losses to non-performing loans did not change. 
The conclusion that the ratio increased could be derived if the net charge-offs were added rather than subtracted in calculating the allowance for loan losses at the end of the year.
Allowance for loan losses at start of year	1,500
Add: Provision for loan losses during the year	500
Add: Net charge-offs during the year	200
Allowance for loan losses at end of year	2,200
Then the calculation of the ratio of allowances for loan losses to non-performing loans becomes;
 	Start of Year	End of Year
Allowances for loan losses	1,500	2,200
Non-performing loans	2,000	2,400
Ratio	0.75	0.92

questions.q: Regarding Plan A, which of the following would be recognized as an expense on Gowran's income statement?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because under IFRS, remeasurements are recognized in other comprehensive income on the balance sheet, not as a pension expense in the income statement. 
In contrast, under US GAAP, all actuarial gains and losses and differences between the expected and actual return on pension assets (remeasurements in IFRS) can be reported either in P&L or, the more commonly chosen approach, in OCI and amortized to the income statement.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because under IFRS, pension expense does not consider employer’s contributions to the plan (nor the settlement of benefits via payments to retirees); it is a non-cash accrual based on the change in the net pension liability or asset. Plan contributions are recognized on the statement of cash flows, typically in operating activities.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Based on Carter's assumptions regarding the exercise of the share options, paid-in capital on Gowran's balance sheet in the current year will increase by:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this ignores the $6 million transferred from share-based compensation reserve to paid-in capital and only considers the $24 million amount which is 2 million options at $12 strike price.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the adjustment to paid-in capital is incorrectly calculated as a $36 million increase which is based on 2 million options exercised at the current share price of $18 (rather than using the strike price of $12) plus the $6 million transferred from share-based compensation reserve.
